blocks.html: A probability distribution is the complete description of how probability is spread over a random variable’s values: a PMF for a discrete variable, a PDF for a continuous one. A few shapes recur so often that they have names and are fixed by one or two parameters (the Binomial by n and p; the Normal by μ and σ). Knowing the name and the parameters determines every probability. §5.7.1 covers the discrete family (Bernoulli, binomial, Poisson); §5.7.2 covers the continuous family (uniform, Normal, and the t, chi-square and F distributions that inference is built on).
Discrete Distributions

Three named distributions cover most counts in community medicine: a single yes/no trial (Bernoulli, §5.7.1.1), the number of successes in a fixed number of independent trials (binomial, §5.7.1.2), and the number of events in a fixed stretch of time or space (Poisson, §5.7.1.3). The binomial is built from Bernoulli trials, and the Poisson is the binomial’s limit when trials are many and each is unlikely.
Bernoulli Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A Bernoulli random variable takes the value 1 (“success”) with probability p and 0 (“failure”) with probability 1 − p.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: This is one yes/no outcome: CBHI member or not, vaccinated or not, survived or died. The two outcomes need not be equally likely. It is the building block of the binomial.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
From the definitions in §5.6.1:

E(X) = 1 × p + 0 × (1 − p) = p.

Var(X) = (1 − p)² × p + (0 − p)² × (1 − p) = p(1 − p)[(1 − p) + p] = p(1 − p).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: One patient recovers with probability p = 0.8. Recovery is Bernoulli(0.8): mean 0.8, variance 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.16.

points.html: Mean = p; variance = p(1 − p). The variance is largest at p = 0.5.
Any single binary outcome in a dataset is one Bernoulli trial.

blocks.html: Binomial Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A binomial random variable X counts the successes in n trials that are independent and share the same success probability p. Its PMF is

P(X = k) = C(n, k) × pᵏ × (1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ, for k = 0, 1, … , n,

where C(n, k) = n! ÷ [k!(n − k)!] is the number of ways of choosing which k of the n trials are the successes.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: X is the sum of n independent Bernoulli trials. To get the probability of exactly k successes you need two things: the probability of any one particular sequence with k successes, and the number of such sequences. The counting rules below supply the second.

blocks.label: Derivation: counting rules
blocks.html:
Factorial. The number of ways to arrange n distinct items in a row is n! = n × (n − 1) × … × 2 × 1 (“n factorial”). There are n choices for the first place, n − 1 for the second, and so on. By convention 0! = 1 (there is exactly one way to arrange nothing). Example: 5! = 120.

Permutations. The number of ordered selections of r items from n is ⁿPᵣ = n × (n − 1) × … × (n − r + 1) = n! ÷ (n − r)!. Example: choosing a chairperson and a secretary from 4 ASHAs, ⁴P₂ = 4 × 3 = 12.

Combinations. If order does not matter, each unordered group of r has been counted r! times among the permutations. So ⁿCᵣ = C(n, r) = n! ÷ [r!(n − r)!]. Example: choosing 2 ASHAs for training from 4, C(4, 2) = 12 ÷ 2! = 6.

blocks.label: Derivation: the binomial PMF
blocks.html:
1. Take one particular sequence with k successes and n − k failures, say S S F … F. Its trials are independent, so by the multiplication rule its probability is p × p × (1 − p) × … = pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ. Every sequence with k successes has this same probability, whatever the order.
  2. Different sequences are different outcomes, so they are mutually exclusive. By the addition rule, P(X = k) = (number of such sequences) × pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ.
  3. A sequence is fixed by choosing which k of the n positions hold the successes: C(n, k) ways.

For n = 3, p = 0.8, k = 2: the sequences are SSF, SFS, FSS, so C(3, 2) = 3 and P(X = 2) = 3 × 0.8² × 0.2 = 0.384.

Mean and variance follow from the Bernoulli results. X is a sum of n Bernoulli variables, and expected values add, so E(X) = np. For independent variables the variances also add (proved in §6.5, rule 3; you can check it numerically below), so Var(X) = np(1 − p).

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
Twenty patients each independently recover with probability 0.8. X ~ Binomial(n = 20, p = 0.8), read “X follows a binomial distribution with n = 20 and p = 0.8”.

  1. C(20, 18) = 20! ÷ (18! × 2!) = (20 × 19) ÷ 2 = 190.
  2. 0.8¹⁸ × 0.2² = 0.000721.
  3. P(X = 18) = 190 × 0.000721 = 0.137.
  4. P(all 20 recover) = 0.8²⁰ = 0.0115, and P(X ≥ 18) = P(18) + P(19) + P(20) = 0.206.
  5. Mean = 20 × 0.8 = 16 recoveries; variance = 20 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 3.2. Computing Σ(k − 16)²P(X = k) over k = 0 to 20 from the PMF also gives 3.2, the numerical check of the variance rule.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.3. Binomial(20, 0.8): the bar at 18 has height 0.137; the distribution peaks at 16, the mean.

points.html: P(X = k) = C(n, k)pᵏ(1 − p)ⁿ⁻ᵏ; mean np; variance np(1 − p).
Two conditions: independent trials (§5.4) and the same p for every trial. Infections passing between patients, or recovery chances that differ by severity, break the plain binomial model.

As n grows the binomial’s shape approaches the Normal curve. §5.7.2.2.4 turns this into a working approximation, and the Central Limit Theorem (sums of many independent variables tend to a Normal shape, §6.6) explains it.
The binomial underlies the sign test (a test that counts how many paired differences are positive, §10.1.1) and exact confidence intervals for a proportion (§7.2.4).

blocks.html: Poisson Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
A Poisson random variable counts events in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur at a constant average rate λ (“lambda”) per interval. Its PMF is

P(X = k) = e^(−λ) × λᵏ ÷ k!, for k = 0, 1, 2, …

where e = 2.71828… is the constant defined in the derivation below.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Some counts have no natural number of trials: new cancer diagnoses in a district in a month, road-traffic deaths on a highway in a week. The Poisson model needs only the average rate. It rests on three assumptions about the process: (1) events occur at a constant rate over the interval; (2) events occur independently of one another; (3) two events do not happen at exactly the same instant. “Rare” is not one of the assumptions. It matters only when the Poisson is used to approximate a binomial, as in the derivation.

blocks.label: Derivation: the Poisson as the limit of the binomial
blocks.html:
Divide the month into n tiny slots, so small that each holds at most one event, with probability p = λ/n in each. The count is then Binomial(n, λ/n), and

P(X = k) = C(n, k)(λ/n)ᵏ(1 − λ/n)ⁿ⁻ᵏ = [n(n − 1)…(n − k + 1) ÷ nᵏ] × (λᵏ ÷ k!) × (1 − λ/n)ⁿ × (1 − λ/n)⁻ᵏ.

Let n grow without limit, with k fixed:

  1. n(n − 1)…(n − k + 1) ÷ nᵏ → 1 (each of the k factors n, n − 1, … divided by n tends to 1).
  2. (1 − λ/n)⁻ᵏ → 1.
  3. (1 − λ/n)ⁿ → e^(−λ). Here e is defined as the limit of (1 + 1/n)ⁿ as n grows: 2.594 at n = 10, 2.705 at n = 100, 2.717 at n = 1,000, approaching 2.71828. That (1 − λ/n)ⁿ tends to e raised to the power −λ is a standard limit (proof beyond this book); you can check it numerically: with λ = 3, (1 − 3/1,000)¹⁰⁰⁰ = 0.0496, against e^(−3) = 0.0498.

What remains is e^(−λ)λᵏ ÷ k!. Because the binomial mean np = λ stays fixed while its variance np(1 − λ/n) tends to λ, the Poisson has mean = variance = λ.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation
blocks.html:
A district records an average of λ = 3 new childhood cancer diagnoses per month.

  1. P(X = 0) = e^(−3) = 0.050.
  2. P(X = 5) = e^(−3) × 3⁵ ÷ 5! = 0.0498 × 243 ÷ 120 = 0.101.
  3. P(at least one) = 1 − 0.050 = 0.950 (complement rule).
  4. Binomial check: with n = 3,000 slots and p = 0.001, Binomial P(X = 5) = 0.1008, the same as the Poisson to four places; with n = 30 and p = 0.1 it is 0.1023.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.4. Poisson(3): P(0) = 0.050, P(5) = 0.101; mean and variance both 3.

points.html: P(X = k) = e^(−λ)λᵏ ÷ k!; mean = variance = λ.

If the observed variance of counts is much larger than the mean (overdispersion), the independence or constant-rate assumption has failed, and the negative binomial model (§13.6) is the standard alternative.

Does the model apply? Cases in an infectious outbreak are not independent: each case can cause others, so cases arrive in clusters and counts are overdispersed. The Poisson suits non-contagious events such as cancer diagnoses or road-traffic deaths, not outbreak case counts.
Poisson approximates the binomial when n is large and p small; one published rule of thumb asks for n ≥ 20 and p ≤ 0.05 (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, n.d.).
Poisson counts per unit of person-time are rates, the basis of §7.4 and Poisson regression (§13.5).

questions.prompt: Explain how a binomial random variable is a sum of Bernoulli trials. For n = 20, p = 0.8, state the mean and variance and show where they come from.
questions.answer: Code each patient 1 (recovers) or 0 (does not): each is Bernoulli(0.8). The number who recover is the sum of the 20 codes, and that sum is Binomial(20, 0.8) when the patients are independent with the same p. Expected values add: mean = 20 × 0.8 = 16. Variances of independent variables add: variance = 20 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 3.2 (SD 1.79).

questions.prompt: Why is the Poisson distribution a reasonable model for “number of new cancer diagnoses in a district per month” but not for “number of patients who recover out of 20 treated”? Why would “number of cases per week in a measles outbreak” usually be overdispersed?
questions.answer: New cancer diagnoses in a district occur one at a time, roughly independently, at a fairly steady rate, with no fixed number of trials: the Poisson assumptions. Recoveries out of 20 have a fixed number of trials (20) and a success probability per patient, which is the binomial set-up, and the count cannot exceed 20. Measles cases are contagious: each case raises the chance of further cases, so cases arrive in bursts. Some weeks have many and others none, and the variance of weekly counts exceeds the mean (overdispersion), breaking the independence assumption.

questions.prompt: Road-traffic deaths on a stretch of highway average λ = 2 per month. Find P(no deaths next month) and P(at least one).

blocks.html: Continuous Distributions

The uniform distribution (§5.7.2.1) is the simplest continuous shape. The Normal distribution (§5.7.2.2) describes some measurements approximately and, more importantly, the behaviour of sample means (§6.6); its subsections turn it into z-scores, reference ranges, growth standards and approximations for counts. The t, chi-square and F distributions (§5.7.2.3–§5.7.2.5) are built from standard Normal variables. They rarely describe raw data; they describe statistics calculated from samples, and they supply the multipliers and cut-offs for confidence intervals and tests.
Uniform Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A uniform random variable on [a, b] has constant density 1 ÷ (b − a) between a and b and zero elsewhere.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: It is the continuous version of the fair die. Every point in [a, b] is equally likely, so the probability of a sub-interval depends only on its width: P(c ≤ X ≤ d) = (d − c) ÷ (b − a).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: A random-number generator producing values in [0, 1] is Uniform(0, 1). P(0.2 ≤ X ≤ 0.3) = 0.1 = P(0.7 ≤ X ≤ 0.8). This is how software draws random samples and allocates participants at random.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.5. Uniform(0, 1): a flat density of height 1.

points.html: Mean = (a + b) ÷ 2; variance = (b − a)² ÷ 12.
Biological measurements seldom look uniform; its uses are in simulation and random allocation.

blocks.html: Normal Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
The Normal (Gaussian) distribution with mean μ and standard deviation σ is the continuous, symmetric, bell-shaped distribution with density

f(x) = [1 ÷ (σ√(2π))] × e^(−(x − μ)² ÷ (2σ²)).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The density is highest at μ and falls away symmetrically; σ sets the width. Some measurements in a homogeneous population are close to Normal, adult height being the standard example. Many are not: many laboratory analytes are skewed, which is why laboratories often transform them before calculating reference limits (Ozarda, 2016; §5.7.2.2.3). The Normal distribution’s central role comes from elsewhere. The means of samples tend towards a Normal shape as sample size grows, whatever the shape of the raw variable (the Central Limit Theorem, §6.6), and that is what most confidence intervals and tests rely on.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Adult height in a population is close to Normal with μ = 165 cm and σ = 7 cm: most people are near 165 cm, and very short and very tall people are equally rare.

blocks.alt: A Normal distribution — mean 165 cm, SD 7 cm
blocks.caption: Figure 5.6. A Normal distribution with mean 165 cm and SD 7 cm.

points.html: Fully specified by μ and σ.
Symmetric, so mean = median = mode (recall §2.5 and §3.9).
Probabilities for any range come from converting to z-scores and reading the standard Normal table (§5.7.2.2.1). The empirical rule (§5.7.2.2.2) is a rounded summary of that table.
Check shape before assuming normality: a histogram (recall §4.3) or a Normal plot (§9.3) of the raw variable.

blocks.html: Z-Score and Standardisation

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A z-score states how many standard deviations a value lies from the mean: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ. Standardisation converts every value of a variable to its z-score. If X is Normal(μ, σ), then Z = (X − μ) ÷ σ is standard Normal: Normal with mean 0 and SD 1.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Each Normal variable has its own mean and SD, so a raw value on its own tells you little. Subtracting the mean and dividing by the SD puts every variable on one unit-free scale, “SDs from the mean”. A single table of the standard Normal, the z-table, then answers probability questions for any Normal variable.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In a hypothetical population of children with mean weight 11 kg and SD 1 kg, a child weighing 13 kg has z = (13 − 11) ÷ 1 = +2. The z-table gives P(Z < 2) = 0.977, so the child is heavier than about 97.7% of the population. If the same population’s height has mean 86 cm and SD 3.5 cm, the child’s height of 90 cm gives z = (90 − 86) ÷ 3.5 = +1.14 (P(Z < 1.14) = 0.873). Kilograms and centimetres cannot be compared directly, but on the z scale the child is more unusual for weight (+2) than for height (+1.14). The comparison into percentages is valid only if both variables are close to Normal; for skewed variables, §5.7.2.2.3 shows the adjustment used for children’s weight.

blocks.alt: The standard normal distribution and a z-score
blocks.caption: Figure 5.7. The standard Normal curve with z = +2 marked; the shaded tail holds 2.3% of the area.

points.html: z = (x − μ) ÷ σ for a population value; z = (x − x̄) ÷ s when the mean and SD are estimated from a sample.
z = 0 at the mean; positive above, negative below.

Reading the z-table: the table lists P(Z ≤ z). The value with 97.5% of the area below it is z = 1.96, so 95% of the area lies between −1.96 and +1.96. That 1.96 is the multiplier in 95% confidence intervals (§7.2).
A z-score describes position, not normality or abnormality. Whether z = −2 matters clinically is a separate judgement.

blocks.html: Empirical Rule (68-95-99.7)

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: The empirical rule is a rounded summary of the standard Normal table: about 68% of a Normal distribution lies within 1 SD of the mean, about 95% within 2 SD, and about 99.7% within 3 SD.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The rule gives an instant sense of how unusual a distance from the mean is, without a table. It is a rounding. The exact areas are 68.27%, 95.45% and 99.73%, and exactly 95% lies within ±1.96 SD. Use ±2 for a quick mental estimate and ±1.96 whenever you calculate.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: With adult height μ = 165 cm and σ = 7 cm, the rule says roughly 95% of adults are between 165 − 2 × 7 = 151 cm and 179 cm. The exact 95% range is 165 ± 1.96 × 7 = 151.3 to 178.7 cm. About 2.3% of adults (the area above z = 2) are taller than 179 cm.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.8. The empirical rule for height (mean 165 cm, SD 7 cm): ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD hold about 68%, 95% and 99.7% of adults.

points.html: ±1 SD ≈ 68.3%; ±2 SD ≈ 95.4%; ±3 SD ≈ 99.7%. Exactly 95% lies within ±1.96 SD.

Values beyond ±2 SD are sometimes flagged as “unusual” in exploratory work. This is an informal cousin of the significance level α = 0.05 (the tolerated probability of a false-positive conclusion in a hypothesis test, §8.4), not the same thing.
The rule applies only to a Normal distribution. For a skewed variable the shares within ±1, ±2 and ±3 SD can be quite different.

questions.prompt: A colleague says a z-score of −2 means “something is wrong”. Explain precisely what z = −2 tells you and what it does not.
questions.answer: The value lies 2 standard deviations below the mean of its reference distribution. If that distribution is Normal, about 2.3% of the reference population lie lower. It does not by itself mean disease or that “something is wrong”: that needs clinical context and, where relevant, an agreed cut-off (such as the WHO −2 growth cut-offs of §5.7.2.2.3).

questions.prompt: What percentage of a Normal variable lies more than 2 SD from the mean in either direction? Give the empirical-rule answer and the exact answer, and say which multiplier gives exactly 5%.
questions.answer: Empirical rule: about 100 − 95 = 5%. Exactly: 100 − 95.45 = 4.55% (2.275% in each tail). Exactly 5% lies beyond ±1.96 SD.

questions.prompt: Adult height is Normal with mean 165 cm and SD 7 cm. What percentage of adults are taller than 179 cm?

blocks.html: Reference Ranges, Centiles and Growth Z-Scores

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: A reference interval (reference range) is the range that contains a stated central share, conventionally the central 95%, of values in a defined healthy reference population. Its limits are the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles (percentiles; recall §3.3). A growth z-score is a child’s z-score calculated against the median and spread of a growth standard for the same age and sex: height-for-age (HAZ), weight-for-age (WAZ) and weight-for-height (WHZ).

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A laboratory’s “normal range” answers the question: where do healthy people’s values lie? The convention sets the limits at the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles of healthy people, and so, by construction, 5% of healthy people fall outside it and are flagged (Ozarda, 2016). If the analyte is Normal in healthy people, those centiles are μ ± 1.96σ. If it is skewed, μ ± 1.96σ puts the limits in the wrong places, and the laboratory either reads the centiles directly from the data (the non-parametric method) or transforms the values (often by logarithm) until they are Normal, calculates μ ± 1.96σ on that scale and transforms back (Ozarda, 2016).

Growth charts apply the same idea to children, with the reference changing month by month. The WHO Child Growth Standards tabulate, for every month of age and each sex, the median and the spread of healthy growth, and a child is located by a z-score against them. Stunting is HAZ below −2, underweight is WAZ below −2 and wasting is WHZ below −2, each measured from the median of the WHO Child Growth Standards (WHO Global Health Observatory, n.d.); a z-score below −3 marks the severe form (severe stunting, severe underweight, severe wasting; Boua et al., 2023, Table 1).

For height, the WHO table’s distribution is symmetric at each age, so HAZ = (height − median) ÷ SD. Weight is right-skewed, so a single SD does not fit both sides. The WHO tables use the LMS method (Cole & Green, 1992), which summarises the distribution at each age by three numbers: M (the median), S (a coefficient of variation) and L (a power that removes the skewness, a Box–Cox power). The z-score is

z = [(y ÷ M)^L − 1] ÷ (L × S),

which reduces to (y − M) ÷ (M × S), an ordinary z-score, when L = 1.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 1: a skewed laboratory value
blocks.html:
Suppose serum triglyceride in a healthy reference population is right-skewed, with its logarithm Normal: median 110 mg/dL and SD of ln(value) 0.45 (hypothetical figures).

  1. On the original scale the mean is 121.7 mg/dL and the SD 57.7 mg/dL.
  2. Naive interval: 121.7 ± 1.96 × 57.7 = 8.7 to 234.8 mg/dL. The lower limit is far below any healthy value, and 4.6% (not 2.5%) of healthy people lie above the upper limit.
  3. Log method: exp(ln 110 ± 1.96 × 0.45) = 45.5 to 265.7 mg/dL, which contains exactly the central 95%.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 2: height-for-age (WHO table, L = 1)
blocks.html:
A boy aged 30 months measures 84.0 cm. The WHO height-for-age table for boys at 30 months gives median 91.9327 cm and SD 3.4052 cm.

  1. HAZ = (84.0 − 91.9327) ÷ 3.4052 = −2.33.
  2. −2.33 is below −2 but above −3, so the boy is stunted, not severely (the −2 and −3 SD heights at 30 months are 85.1 and 81.7 cm).
  3. As a centile: P(Z < −2.33) = 0.0099, the 1st centile. As a percentage of the median: 84.0 ÷ 91.93 = 91.4%.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 3: weight-for-age (WHO table, L ≠ 1)
blocks.html:
For boys aged 24 months the WHO weight-for-age table gives L = −0.0137, M = 12.1515 kg, S = 0.11426. A boy of that age weighs 9.0 kg.

  1. (9.0 ÷ 12.1515)^(−0.0137) = 1.00412.
  2. WAZ = (1.00412 − 1) ÷ (−0.0137 × 0.11426) = −2.63: underweight, not severely.
  3. The skew shows in the table itself: the −2 z-score weight is 2.48 kg below the median (9.67 kg), but the +2 z-score weight is 3.13 kg above it (15.28 kg). A naive (9.0 − 12.15) ÷ (12.15 × 0.114) would give −2.27 and understate how light the child is.
  4. Check: inverting the formula, y = M(1 + L × S × z)^(1/L), gives 9.67 kg at z = −2 and 8.63 kg at z = −3, matching the WHO table’s printed 9.7 and 8.6 kg.

blocks.alt: WHO height-for-age z-score lines for boys aged 2–5 years, with the worked example
blocks.caption: Figure 5.9. WHO height-for-age standard for boys, 24–60 months. The boy of Worked Calculation 2 (30 months, 84.0 cm) sits between the −2 and −3 lines: HAZ −2.33, stunted.

points.html: A reference interval is descriptive of health, not a diagnostic threshold. 5% of healthy people fall outside it by construction, and if a healthy person has 20 independent tests, the chance that at least one is flagged is 1 − 0.95²⁰ = 64%. Clinical decision limits (thresholds tied to outcomes or treatment) are a different thing and should not be confused with reference limits (Ozarda, 2016).
Use μ ± 1.96σ only when the analyte is close to Normal in the reference group; otherwise use centiles or a transformation.
Stunting, underweight and wasting: HAZ, WAZ, WHZ < −2; severe: < −3 (WHO Child Growth Standards).

z-score, centile and percentage of median are three ways of saying where a child sits. The z-score is equally spaced at the extremes: z = −2 and z = −3 are 1 SD apart, but they correspond to the 2.3rd and the 0.13th centiles, which look almost identical on a centile scale. Percentage of median does not account for the spread at each age, so the same percentage means a different z-score at different ages.

Growth z-scores in surveys are summarised like any other variable: prevalence of z < −2, and the mean z-score of the population. WHO’s LMS tables mean you should use software built on them rather than hand calculation for large datasets.

blocks.html: Normal Approximations to Binomial and Poisson

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: For large enough counts, a binomial variable X ~ Binomial(n, p) is approximately Normal with mean np and SD √[np(1 − p)], and a Poisson variable X ~ Poisson(λ) is approximately Normal with mean λ and SD √λ. The continuity correction adds or subtracts 0.5 at the boundary when a discrete count is approximated by a continuous curve.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Before computers, binomial and Poisson tail probabilities with large n or λ were tedious sums, so they were read from the Normal curve instead. The approximation still matters because it is the reason the simple z-based confidence interval for a proportion (§7.2.2) and the chi-square test (§10.6) work. The approximation is good when the distribution is not piled up against 0 or n. A widely used criterion for the binomial is that both np and n(1 − p) are at least 5 (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, n.d.); for the Poisson, a mean of at least 5 is quoted as adequate (NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook, n.d.), and larger is better. The continuity correction treats the bar for count k as the interval k − 0.5 to k + 0.5.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html: The mean and SD are those already derived for each distribution (§5.7.1.2 and §5.7.1.3). The Normal shape follows because a binomial count is a sum of n independent Bernoulli variables, and sums of many independent variables tend to a Normal shape (the Central Limit Theorem, §6.6). A Poisson(λ) count is the sum of λ independent Poisson(1) counts when λ is a whole number (independent Poisson counts add to a Poisson count; proof beyond this book), so the same argument applies as λ grows.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 1: binomial
blocks.html:
In villages where 30% of households are CBHI members, a supervisor visits 50 households. What is P(10 or fewer members)?

  1. np = 15 and n(1 − p) = 35, both ≥ 5. Mean 15, SD = √(50 × 0.3 × 0.7) = 3.24.
  2. With continuity correction: z = (10.5 − 15) ÷ 3.24 = −1.39; P(Z < −1.39) = 0.082.
  3. Without it: z = (10 − 15) ÷ 3.24 = −1.54; P = 0.061.
  4. Exact binomial sum: 0.079. The corrected approximation is off by 0.004; the uncorrected one by 0.018.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.10. Binomial(50, 0.3) bars with the Normal curve (mean 15, SD 3.24). The bars for 0–10 end at 10.5, which is why the continuity correction cuts the curve there.

blocks.label: Worked Calculation 2: Poisson
blocks.html:
A district averages λ = 20 road-traffic deaths a month. What is P(30 or more next month)?

  1. Mean 20, SD √20 = 4.47.
  2. With continuity correction: z = (29.5 − 20) ÷ 4.47 = 2.12; P(Z > 2.12) = 0.017.
  3. Exact Poisson sum: 0.022. The approximation is in the right region but understates the upper tail, because a Poisson with λ = 20 is still slightly right-skewed. For tail probabilities, use exact calculation when software is available.

points.html: Binomial ≈ Normal(np, √[np(1 − p)]); Poisson ≈ Normal(λ, √λ).
Conditions (a convention): np and n(1 − p) ≥ 5 for the binomial; λ ≥ 5 for the Poisson, better if larger. With n = 20 and p = 0.05, np = 1, and the approximation fails.
Use the continuity correction: P(X ≤ k) ≈ P(Z < (k + 0.5 − mean) ÷ SD); P(X ≥ k) ≈ P(Z > (k − 0.5 − mean) ÷ SD).

Approximations are least accurate in the far tails, which is often where p-values (the probability, if nothing is going on, of a result at least this extreme; §8.5) live. Software gives exact binomial and Poisson probabilities (§7.2.4, §10.1.1).

questions.prompt: A boy aged 36 months measures 88.0 cm. The WHO height-for-age table gives median 96.0835 cm and SD 3.7069 cm at that age. Calculate his HAZ, classify him, and give his approximate centile.
questions.answer: HAZ = (88.0 − 96.0835) ÷ 3.7069 = −8.0835 ÷ 3.7069 = −2.18. Below −2 but not below −3: stunted (moderate), not severely stunted. Centile: P(Z < −2.18) = 0.0146, about the 1.5th centile.

questions.prompt: A laboratory reports a “normal range” for serum ALT. Explain why a healthy person can fall outside it, and why μ ± 1.96σ may be the wrong way to calculate the range.
questions.answer: A reference interval is set at the 2.5th and 97.5th centiles of healthy people, so 5% of healthy people fall outside it by construction. μ ± 1.96σ gives those centiles only if the analyte is Normal in healthy people. Many analytes are skewed in healthy people (Ozarda, 2016); if ALT is, the laboratory should read the centiles directly or transform the values (for example, take logarithms), calculate the limits on that scale and transform back (Ozarda, 2016).

questions.prompt: Twenty per cent of children in a district are anaemic. In a random sample of 100 children, use the Normal approximation with continuity correction to find P(30 or more anaemic). Check the condition first.
questions.answer: Condition: np = 20 and n(1 − p) = 80, both ≥ 5. Mean = 20; SD = √(100 × 0.2 × 0.8) = 4.0. P(X ≥ 30) ≈ P(Z > (29.5 − 20) ÷ 4) = P(Z > 2.375) = 0.009. (The exact binomial value is 0.011: the approximation is close but slightly understates this far tail.)

blocks.html: t-Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html:
If Z is standard Normal and V is an independent sum of the squares of ν independent standard Normal variables (the chi-square variable of §5.7.2.4), then

T = Z ÷ √(V ÷ ν)

has a t-distribution with ν degrees of freedom. It is symmetric and bell-shaped like the standard Normal but has heavier tails.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: The z-score (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) uses the true σ. In practice σ is unknown and you replace it with the sample SD s. The denominator is now itself random: a small sample can give an s that happens to be too small, which makes the ratio too large. The t-distribution builds that extra uncertainty in, through the random V in its denominator, and pays for it with heavier tails. The more data s is based on, the less V ÷ ν varies around 1, and the closer t comes to the standard Normal.

blocks.label: Derivation
blocks.html:
When the observations are drawn from a Normal population with mean μ and SD σ:

  1. Z = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n) is standard Normal. (σ ÷ √n is the standard error of the mean, the SD of x̄ over repeated samples, derived in §6.5 and §6.7.)
  2. V = (n − 1)s² ÷ σ² is chi-square with n − 1 degrees of freedom, and it is independent of x̄ (both facts are standard results; proof beyond this book).
  3. Divide: Z ÷ √(V ÷ (n − 1)) = [(x̄ − μ) ÷ (σ ÷ √n)] ÷ (s ÷ σ) = (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n).

The unknown σ cancels. The familiar ratio (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n) therefore has a t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom (recall degrees of freedom, §3.6.3).

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html:
Ten patients’ systolic BP has mean 128 mmHg and SD s = 12 mmHg. The standard error is 12 ÷ √10 = 3.79 mmHg. The 97.5% point of t with 9 degrees of freedom is 2.262, not 1.96, so a 95% interval for the mean is 128 ± 2.262 × 3.79 = 128 ± 8.6 mmHg, 15% wider than the ±7.4 that 1.96 would give (§7.2.1 builds this interval). The 97.5% points for other degrees of freedom:

df 4 9 29 99 1,000 ∞ (Normal)
t (97.5%) 2.776 2.262 2.045 1.984 1.962 1.960

blocks.alt: The t-distribution at different degrees of freedom, converging to Normal
blocks.caption: Figure 5.11. t-distributions with increasing degrees of freedom approach the standard Normal curve.

points.html: T = Z ÷ √(V ÷ ν); for one sample, (x̄ − μ) ÷ (s ÷ √n) ~ t with n − 1 df.

Use t whenever σ is estimated from the data, at any sample size. The exact result assumes the population is Normal; for larger n the Central Limit Theorem (§6.6) makes the t-based interval approximately right even for non-Normal data. “Small sample → t, large sample → z” is a poor summary: with n = 30 the multiplier is still 2.045.
Heavier tails mean wider intervals: with 9 df, 8.2% of the t-distribution lies beyond ±1.96, not 5%.
The t-distribution underlies the t-tests of §9.2 and the tests of regression coefficients (Chapter 12).

blocks.html: Chi-Square Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: If Z₁, Z₂, … , Z_ν are independent standard Normal variables, then V = Z₁² + Z₂² + … + Z_ν² has a chi-square (χ²) distribution with ν degrees of freedom. It is never negative and is right-skewed; its mean is ν.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Squaring deviations made variance tractable (recall §3.6). The chi-square distribution describes a sum of squared standardised deviations. Squares cannot be negative, so the distribution starts at 0. Small sums are common, and now and then one large squared deviation pushes the sum far to the right. With more terms the sum becomes less skewed.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: With ν = 1, V = Z², and P(Z² > 1.96²) = P(|Z| > 1.96) = 0.05. So the 95% point of χ² with 1 df is 1.96² = 3.841, exactly the tabulated value. With ν = 5 the 95% point is 11.07. The chi-square test of association (§10.6) compares observed counts O with the counts E expected when the null hypothesis (the assumption of no association that a test tries to discredit, §8.2) is true, by squaring each difference, dividing by the expected count and summing: X² = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E. Under the null hypothesis, X² is approximately χ² when expected counts are large enough.

blocks.alt: The chi-square distribution at different degrees of freedom
blocks.caption: Figure 5.12. Chi-square densities: strongly right-skewed with few degrees of freedom, more symmetric with more.

points.html: χ²_ν = sum of ν squared independent standard Normals; mean ν; never negative.
χ²₁ is the square of a z: its 95% point 3.841 = 1.96².
Uses: the chi-square tests for categorical data (§10.6) and confidence intervals for a variance, through (n − 1)s² ÷ σ² ~ χ²ₙ₋₁ for Normal data.

blocks.html: F-Distribution

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: If V₁ and V₂ are independent chi-square variables with ν₁ and ν₂ degrees of freedom, then F = (V₁ ÷ ν₁) ÷ (V₂ ÷ ν₂) has an F-distribution with (ν₁, ν₂) degrees of freedom. It is never negative and right-skewed.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: Each V ÷ ν is a scaled estimate of variance. F compares two of them as a ratio. If the two variances are equal, F is near 1; a large F says the numerator variance is bigger. This is the comparison ANOVA (analysis of variance, the comparison of several group means, §9.5) makes: variation between group means against variation within groups.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Three treatment groups of 10 patients each: ANOVA’s ratio has (2, 27) degrees of freedom, and its 95% point is 3.35. An observed F above 3.35 would be unusual if all three groups shared one mean. A useful identity links the family: t with ν df, squared, is F with (1, ν) df. The 95% point of F(1, 9) is 5.117 = 2.262², the square of the t multiplier in §5.7.2.3.

blocks.caption: Figure 5.13. An F-distribution with (5, 20) degrees of freedom: never negative, right-skewed, fixed by two degrees of freedom.

points.html: F = (V₁ ÷ ν₁) ÷ (V₂ ÷ ν₂); two degrees of freedom, numerator first.
t²_ν = F(1, ν); z² = χ²₁. The four distributions of §5.7.2.2–§5.7.2.5 are one family built from standard Normal variables.
Uses: ANOVA (§9.5), comparing two variances (§9.2.4), and the overall F-test of a regression model (Chapter 12).

questions.prompt: Explain why the t-distribution looks almost identical to the Normal for a large sample but noticeably different for a small one. Use the construction T = Z ÷ √(V ÷ ν) in your answer.
questions.answer: T = Z ÷ √(V ÷ ν), where V ÷ ν comes from the sample SD. With many degrees of freedom, s is a precise estimate of σ, V ÷ ν stays close to 1, and T behaves like Z. With few degrees of freedom, s can be well above or below σ, so the denominator varies a lot; small values of s produce large values of T, and the tails are heavier. For example, the 97.5% point is 2.776 with 4 df, 2.045 with 29 df and 1.984 with 99 df, against 1.960 for Z.

questions.prompt: What are the t, chi-square and F distributions each built from, and what is each used for?
questions.answer: All are built from independent standard Normal variables. Chi-square is a sum of ν squared standard Normals; t is a standard Normal divided by √(chi-square ÷ its df); F is the ratio of two independent chi-squares, each divided by its df. t is used for means when σ is estimated (t-tests, confidence intervals for means, regression coefficients); chi-square for tests on categorical counts and for inference on a variance; F for comparing variances and for ANOVA and overall regression tests.

questions.prompt: For a sample of 10, the 95% multiplier is 2.262 instead of 1.96. By what percentage does this widen a 95% interval for the mean? Show that 2.262² equals the 95% point of F(1, 9), 5.117.
questions.answer: 2.262 ÷ 1.960 = 1.154, so the interval is about 15% wider. 2.262² = 5.117, the 95% point of F(1, 9): the square of a t with 9 df is an F with (1, 9) df.
